lines.speaker: N
lines.text: You know the story. Two men, a map, a ruler, the modern Middle East drawn in an afternoon.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Here is what the record says instead. That line was never implemented. Mosul, given to France, ended up in British Iraq. Palestine, meant as an international zone, became a British mandate outright.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The borders on the map today were drawn later, by conferences those two men were never invited to.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A century afterward, a militia bulldozed a border and named the video after a map that had already stopped being the map.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Sykes-Picot Agreement. May sixteenth, nineteen sixteen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: December nineteen fifteen, the British War Committee. Sir Mark Sykes is thirty six, has traveled the Ottoman Arab provinces as a tourist and an amateur, and now puts his finger down on a map.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A tourist has just proposed dividing several million people, on the strength of two letters of the alphabet.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: For five weeks Sykes meets Francois Georges-Picot, a French diplomat whose family has pressed France's claims in Syria for a generation. Together they color a map.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A blue zone of direct French control runs along the Syrian and Lebanese coast into Cilicia. A red zone of direct British control takes Basra, Baghdad, and the ports of Haifa and Acre. Between the colors, an Area A and an Area B cover the interior as French and British spheres.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: An independent Arab state, under an Arab chief, inside a zone France and Britain had already colored their own. Signed by the same two men, on the same page.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A year earlier, in letters running from July nineteen fifteen to January nineteen sixteen, Sir Henry McMahon had already told Sharif Hussein of Mecca that Britain was prepared to recognize and support the independence of the Arabs, if the Arabs rose against the Ottomans.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Damascus, Homs, Hama, and Aleppo, the four cities McMahon's letter treats as Arab, sit inside or beside the zone Sykes and Picot had already colored French.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On November second, nineteen seventeen, Arthur James Balfour adds a third claimant to the same territory.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The secret holds eighteen months. In November nineteen seventeen the Bolsheviks find the treaty and publish it. The Manchester Guardian prints it on November twenty sixth.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Ottomans relay the text to Hussein, to prove his allies had betrayed him.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Lawrence had ridden beside the men making that promise. He is not describing someone else's betrayal.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In March nineteen twenty the Syrian National Congress crowns Faisal king of an independent Arab Syria. The San Remo Conference meets that April and hands the zones to France and Britain as League of Nations mandates.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: French troops march on Damascus. On July twenty fourth they crush Faisal's army at Maysalun. War Minister Yusuf al-Azma dies on the field, leading men he already knows will lose.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The border in that video was never the line Sykes and Picot agreed to. Palestine was to be international. It became a British mandate instead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: One document, three broken promises, and five accounts of who was actually owed this land. Each one gets its own case first.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: From London and Paris this was wartime statecraft, not conspiracy. The Ottoman Empire had entered the war on Germany's side, and Britain and France meant to divide its collapse without turning on each other the way they nearly had at Fashoda in eighteen ninety eight.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Britain's core interest was the route to India, the Suez Canal and the oilfields of Mesopotamia. France held historic claims dating to the Crusades and a colonial lobby that regarded Syria as a French birthright.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The mandate that followed was framed as a sacred trust of civilisation, tutelage toward a readiness the two governments alone would judge. Balfour set that framework down for Lord Curzon.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Later defenders note the map itself barely survived. San Remo, Sevres, and Lausanne replaced its zones with mandates nobody had drawn in nineteen sixteen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: To Arabs, this was the founding betrayal of the modern era. Sharif Hussein did not rise against four centuries of Ottoman rule for a slogan. He negotiated, and in writing, Britain committed to recognize and support the independence of the Arabs in the regions the Sherif of Mecca had named.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: More than five thousand Arab casualties bought that promise. Arab fighters cut the Hejaz railway and took Aqaba and Damascus, fighting to liberate a homeland Sykes and Picot had already finished dividing a month before the revolt began.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Damascus, Homs, Hama, and Aleppo, the same cities McMahon's own letter had called Arab, sat beside the zone the two diplomats had colored French.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: George Antonius, the movement's first great historian, gave the agreement a name.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Hussein learned the treaty existed from his own enemy's press, and kept fighting anyway.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: For the Zionist movement the decisive document was not the secret map but the public letter that followed it. Sykes-Picot had consigned Palestine to a murky international zone that gave the Jewish national project nothing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Chaim Weizmann, a chemist whose acetone process had aided the British war effort, spent years cultivating ministers and editors, arguing that a Jewish Palestine would answer nearly two thousand years of exile.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That condition was never met, and the agreement collapsed with it. But to Zionists it still showed the two movements were not fated to collide, and that Britain betrayed the Jewish national home too, restricting immigration in the nineteen thirty nine White Paper exactly when European Jews needed refuge most.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Beneath the argument between Arab kings, French generals, and Zionist diplomats were the people who actually lived on the land, and for most of them the new borders were an act of erasure.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Kurds fared worst. Promised a state at Sevres, denied one at Lausanne, they were split among Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran, and became the largest stateless nation on earth.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Druze of the Hawran had governed their own mountain for generations. Under French mandate rule they rose in nineteen twenty five behind Sultan al-Atrash.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: France answered with aircraft and colonial troops, and shelled Damascus itself. At least six thousand rebels were killed. Iraq was assembled from three Ottoman provinces that had never been governed as one, and handed to a king imported from the Hejaz.

segments.title: Peoples of the Levant and Mesopotamia

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A century on, scholars are divided over how much this one agreement actually explains. David Fromkin's telling made the popular case.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A revisionist current pushes back. The map was never implemented as drawn. Mosul, assigned to France, ended up in British Iraq. Palestine, meant to be international, became a British mandate instead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: To call Arab states uniquely artificial, these historians argue, is to imply Arabs are uniquely incapable of building nations. Iraq's tensions were governed and exploited for a century by Iraqis themselves, not by a line on a map.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The lasting damage, in this reading, was the mandate system: the denial of self-determination, rule by sectarian division, and a pattern of promising one thing and delivering another.

segments.title: Later Scholarship / The Myth and the Line

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And here is what none of the five will say for itself.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Imperial case says nothing about Britain writing three incompatible promises inside two years, and letting the Arabs learn of one from a Bolshevik newspaper.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Arab Nationalist case says less about the ambiguities in McMahon's own wording that Britain later leaned on.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Zionist case says nothing about the ninety percent of Palestine's population that commitment was made without asking.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The case for the peoples of the Levant says less about the local elites who collaborated with the mandates for their own advantage.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And the revisionist case, fluent in how the map was redrawn twice before anyone lived under it, has almost nothing to say about how much force that symbol still carries: a militia bulldozing a border in twenty fourteen was not citing footnotes.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Faisal had led the Arab Revolt, been crowned king of an independent Syria, and watched Maysalun burn that kingdom down. Britain installed him instead as king of Iraq: a country assembled from three Ottoman provinces, whose borders he had not drawn and whose peoples he barely knew.
